- Low reuse: a prefix read once never recovers its write premium.
- TTL expiry: a cache that lapses between calls forces a fresh write.

> **Interview.** A strong answer names the mechanism (prefill state reuse), the ordering rule (stable prefix first), and the break-even (reads at 0.1x pay back a 1.25x write in two uses), then connects it to why long context is no longer automatically too expensive.

```recall
Q: Why does putting retrieved RAG context at the top of the prompt destroy caching?
A: Caching keys on a byte-identical prefix. Retrieved context changes per query, so an early variable block invalidates the cache for everything after it, giving zero hits while you still pay the write premium.
Q: With a 1.25x write and 0.1x read, how many reuses break even?
A: Two. 1.25 + 0.1 = 1.35 beats 2.0 for two uncached requests, so from the second read on you are saving.
Q: Why does caching make the 2023 long-context-is-too-expensive argument weaker?
A: The expensive part was re-processing a long repeated prefix every call. Caching serves that prefix from stored state at a fraction of the price, so a long stable context amortizes across reuses.
Q: What does prefill do, and why is it the part caching targets?
A: Prefill reads all input tokens and builds the KV attention state before any output. For a repeated prefix that work is identical each call, so caching stores and replays it.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Why the KV cache is what gets stored

During prefill the model computes, for every input token and every layer, the key and value vectors that later tokens attend to. That is the KV cache. For a fixed prefix those vectors are deterministic, so a provider can serialize them, key them by a hash of the prefix bytes, and restore them on a matching request. Decode then starts immediately against the restored cache. This is why the saving shows up most as time-to-first-token: prefill is skipped, and TTFT is dominated by prefill on long inputs.

## Scope and invalidation

Caches are scoped and short-lived by design. Anthropic uses a sliding TTL (5 minutes default, refreshed on each hit, with a 1-hour option), so an actively reused prefix stays warm while an idle one lapses. The cache is also typically scoped to an organization or account, not shared across tenants, which matters for both correctness and data isolation. Any change inside the cached span, including tool-schema edits mid-conversation, forces a rewrite of the whole span, which is why mid-stream tool changes historically triggered an expensive 12.5x re-process penalty (0.1x read lost, 1.25x write paid).

## Interaction with routing and batching

Caching composes with the other cost levers but can conflict with routing. If a router sends similar requests to different models, each model keeps its own cache, so cache hit rate drops as routing fans out. Batch APIs are a separate discount path (asynchronous, roughly half price) and are usually a better fit than caching for one-shot bulk jobs where there is no repeated prefix to reuse. The decision rule: caching for repeated-prefix interactive traffic, batching for latency-tolerant one-shot volume.

## Measuring it

Instrument cache hit rate as a first-class metric: fraction of input tokens served from cache, and cost per request split into write, read, and uncached buckets. A healthy repeated-prefix workload should see the large majority of prefix tokens as reads. A sudden drop usually means a prefix token started varying. Log the first N bytes of the cached span hash per request so you can diff two requests that should have hit the same cache and find the token that diverged.

lessons.title: Routing, cascades, and batching
lessons.body:
Routing, cascades, and batching are the cost levers you reach for after caching. The core idea: not every request needs a frontier model, and not every request needs to be answered now. Interviewers like these because they force you to reason about cost per request against accuracy and latency, and to say how you would measure that the cheap path is not quietly degrading quality.

## Routing

A router classifies each request and sends it to the cheapest model that can handle it: easy requests to a small fast model, hard ones to a frontier model. This is one of the five named workflow patterns in Anthropic, Building effective agents (2024). The classifier can be a small model call, a heuristic on request features, or embeddings plus nearest-neighbour against labelled examples.

```flow
dir: LR
req: Request | actor
router: Router | gate
small: Small model | model
big: Frontier model | model
req -> router : classify
router -> small : easy
router -> big : hard
small -> req : answer
big -> req : answer
```

The thing that gets tested is evaluation: you must track accuracy split by route and periodically sample the easy bucket for misroutes that actually needed the frontier model. A router that is 2 percent too aggressive can wipe out its own savings in retries and bad answers.

## Cascades

A cascade is a router without an upfront classifier. Try the cheap model first, then escalate only if a confidence or verification check fails. The check can be a self-reported confidence, a validator, a schema check, or a judge.

```steps
Try cheap | Send the request to the small model first
Check | Verify the output with a validator, schema, or confidence score
Escalate | On failure, retry on the frontier model
Return | Return the first answer that passes the check
```

The economics only work when the cheap model succeeds often and the check is cheap and reliable. If the small model fails half the time, you pay for two calls on half your traffic and may be slower than going straight to the frontier model. The verification step is the whole game: a weak check lets bad cheap answers through, an expensive check eats the savings.

## Batching

Batch APIs accept asynchronous, latency-tolerant request batches at a reduced per-token price. OpenAI's Batch API runs within a 24-hour window at a 50 percent cost discount versus the synchronous API (OpenAI docs, as of 2026, re-check). Use it for non-interactive workloads: bulk classification, offline eval runs, dataset generation, backfills.

```bars
title: Batch vs synchronous input cost (OpenAI, illustrative ratio)
unit: x
Synchronous | 1
Batch API | 0.5
```

Batching is orthogonal to caching. Caching helps repeated-prefix interactive traffic; batching helps one-shot bulk volume where latency does not matter. Reach for batching when a human is not waiting.

## Semantic cache

A semantic cache answers a new request from a stored response when the new query is similar enough to a past one, measured by embedding similarity. It can cut cost and latency hard on repetitive traffic.

> **Pitfall.** A semantic cache keys on similarity, not identity, so two prompts that are close in embedding space but need different answers can collide. A high threshold protects correctness but lowers hit rate; a low threshold raises hit rate but serves wrong answers. Tune it against a labelled set and never cache anything personalized or permission-sensitive.

## Trade-offs

| Lever | When it pays | Main risk |
|---|---|---|
| Routing | Mixed easy/hard traffic | Misroutes degrade quality silently |
| Cascade | Cheap model often enough | Double cost when it fails |
| Batching | Latency-tolerant bulk jobs | Up to 24h turnaround |
| Semantic cache | Repetitive queries | Similar query, wrong answer |

## Distillation

Distillation sits further downstream: train a smaller model to imitate a larger one on your task distribution, once you have production data and stable evals. It is not a first move. Reach for it only after prompting, routing, and caching, when you have the data and the eval bar to prove the small model holds up.

> **Interview.** Order the levers: caching first (free, no quality risk), then routing and cascades (cheap-path with a measured guardrail), batching for bulk, semantic cache with a tuned threshold, distillation last. Always pair a cheap path with the metric that proves it is not degrading quality.

```recall
Q: What is the key difference between a router and a cascade?
A: A router classifies upfront and picks a model before calling anything. A cascade tries the cheap model first and escalates only when a verification check fails, so it may pay for two calls on the same request.
Q: Why can a semantic cache serve a wrong answer?
A: It keys on embedding similarity, not exact match, so two close-but-different queries can collide and return a cached response that does not actually fit the new request.
Q: When is batching the right lever instead of caching?
A: When the work is one-shot bulk with no repeated prefix and no human waiting. Caching needs a reused identical prefix; batching trades latency (up to 24h) for roughly half price.
Q: How do you evaluate a router so savings do not hide quality loss?
A: Track accuracy split by route and periodically sample the easy bucket for misroutes that actually needed the frontier model, so you catch a router that is routing too aggressively.
```
lessons.deeper:
## The routing accuracy math

Suppose 70 percent of traffic is genuinely easy and your router sends 75 percent to the small model, meaning 5 percent of total traffic is misrouted hard requests. If a misrouted request produces a wrong answer that triggers a retry on the frontier model, each misroute costs you a wasted small call plus a full frontier call, worse than if you had never routed it. The savings come from the correctly-routed 70 percent paying small-model prices. The decision hinges on the ratio of small-to-frontier price and the misroute rate: savings roughly equal (easy fraction) x (1 - small/frontier price ratio) minus (misroute rate) x (retry overhead). This is why the metric that matters is misroute rate, not raw cost reduction.

## Building the classifier

Three classifier styles, cheapest first. A heuristic on features (length, presence of code, detected intent) is free and transparent but brittle. An embedding plus nearest-neighbour against a labelled example set is cheap, fast, and improves as you add examples, but needs a maintained label set. A small-model classification call is the most flexible and the most expensive of the three; it is still far cheaper than the frontier model it gates. Start with embeddings-plus-kNN when you have labelled examples, because it is both cheap and improvable.

## Confidence signals for cascades

The cascade check needs a signal that correlates with correctness. Options: a schema or validator pass/fail (strong when the task has a verifiable structure), a self-consistency vote across a few cheap samples (escalate on disagreement), a judge model scoring the cheap answer, or token-level logprobs as a rough confidence proxy. Logprob confidence is weak and poorly calibrated on its own; prefer a verifiable check where the task allows one. Whatever the signal, calibrate the escalation threshold on a labelled set and track the escalation rate as an operational metric, because a drifting input distribution will quietly change how often you escalate and therefore your real cost.

## Composing the levers

In production these stack. A typical shape: a semantic cache in front catches repeats, a router splits the misses, both model paths use prompt caching for their stable system prompt, and anything that can tolerate delay goes to a batch queue instead. Each layer has its own metric: cache hit rate, misroute rate, escalation rate, batch turnaround. Treat them as a cost pipeline, measure each stage, and remember that routing can lower cache hit rate by fanning traffic across models, so the levers are not fully independent.

lessons.title: Latency and streaming
lessons.body:
Users do not experience average latency, they experience the first token and the pace after it. The two numbers that matter are time-to-first-token and per-token latency, and they come from different parts of the system, so they are tuned by different levers. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can build a per-stage latency budget and know which lever cuts which stage, rather than reaching for a smaller model for everything.

## TTFT versus per-token latency

Time-to-first-token (TTFT) is how long until the first output token appears. It is dominated by prefill: reading and encoding every input token before decode starts, plus any upstream work (retrieval, routing, network). Per-token latency, often reported as inter-token latency or its inverse tokens-per-second, is how fast tokens come after the first, and it is set by decode, which generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth bound.

```flow
dir: LR
user: User | actor
retr: Retrieval | store
prefill: Prefill | model
decode: Decode loop | model
user -> retr : query
retr -> prefill : context
prefill -> decode : first token
decode -> decode : next token
decode -> user : stream
```

Total latency is roughly: upstream work + prefill (scales with input length) + output length x per-token latency. Long input hurts TTFT; long output hurts total time through the per-token term.

## Streaming

Streaming sends tokens as they are generated instead of waiting for the full response. It does not reduce total time, but it collapses perceived latency: the user sees output at TTFT instead of at completion. For a 600-token answer at 40 tokens per second, non-streaming makes the user wait about 15 seconds for anything; streaming shows the first words in well under a second and then flows.

> **Key idea.** Streaming changes perceived latency, not total latency. The first token is the moment the user stops waiting.

## A per-stage latency budget

Set a target, then split it across stages and attack the fattest one.

```bars
title: Latency budget for one RAG answer (illustrative ms)
unit: ms
Embed query | 40
Vector search | 60
Rerank | 120
Prefill context | 300
First token to user | 180
```

Here prefill plus rerank dominate. The levers follow the budget: if prefill is fat, shorten or cache the context; if rerank is fat, rerank fewer candidates or use a lighter reranker; if decode is the problem, that shows up as a long tail on output length, not in TTFT.

## The levers, matched to the stage

| Lever | Cuts | Cost or limit |
|---|---|---|
| Prompt caching | TTFT (skips prefill) | Needs identical repeated prefix |
| Smaller or distilled model | Per-token and TTFT | Possible quality drop |
| Parallel tool and retrieval calls | Upstream wall time | Only independent calls |
| Shorter output (max tokens, format) | Total via per-token term | May truncate content |
| Streaming | Perceived latency | No change to total |
| Speculative decoding | Per-token | Setup, serving support |

Parallelism matters more than people expect: if a step issues three independent retrieval or tool calls, running them concurrently makes the wall time the max of the three, not the sum.

## Failure modes

- Optimizing average latency while p95 and p99 blow out: tail latency is what users complain about.
- Shrinking the model everywhere, trading quality for speed on requests that did not need it.
- Blocking the stream on a post-hoc validation pass, erasing the perceived-latency win.
- Ignoring output length: a verbose format silently inflates total time through the per-token term.

> **Pitfall.** A guardrail or judge that runs after generation and before the user sees anything turns a streamed response back into a blocking one. Stream first, validate in parallel or on the tail.

> **Interview.** Separate TTFT (prefill, upstream) from per-token (decode, bandwidth), draw a per-stage budget, then name the lever per stage: cache or shorten context for TTFT, parallelize independent calls for upstream, stream for perception, smaller model or speculative decoding for decode. Always talk in percentiles, not averages.

```recall
Q: Why does streaming not reduce total latency but still help users?
A: Tokens are still generated at the same rate, so completion time is unchanged. But the user sees the first token at TTFT instead of at completion, which collapses perceived waiting.
Q: Which stage sets TTFT and which sets per-token latency?
A: TTFT is set by prefill (encoding all input tokens) plus upstream work like retrieval. Per-token latency is set by the decode loop, which generates one token at a time and is memory-bandwidth bound.
Q: You have three independent retrieval calls on the critical path. What is the fix?
A: Run them in parallel so the wall time is the slowest of the three rather than the sum. Only independent calls can be parallelized this way.
Q: Why measure p95 or p99 instead of average latency?
A: Users feel the slow requests. A good average can hide a long tail where a meaningful fraction of requests are painfully slow, which is what drives complaints.
Q: How does a post-generation guardrail hurt latency, and what is the fix?
A: Running a validator after generation and before showing output blocks the stream, erasing the perceived-latency win. Stream the output and run the check in parallel or only on the completed tail.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Why decode is memory-bandwidth bound

Each decode step must read the full model weights and the growing KV cache from GPU memory to produce one token. The arithmetic per token is small relative to the bytes moved, so the step is limited by memory bandwidth, not compute. This is why generating 500 tokens takes roughly 500 times the time of generating one, and why batching many requests together raises throughput (more useful compute per weight read) without lowering any single request's per-token latency. Prefill, by contrast, processes all input tokens in parallel and is compute-bound, which is why a long prompt inflates TTFT but a long output inflates total time through the per-token term.

## Speculative decoding

Speculative decoding uses a small draft model to propose several tokens ahead, which the large model then verifies in a single forward pass. When the draft is right, you get multiple tokens for one large-model step, cutting per-token latency; when it is wrong, you fall back with no correctness loss, since the large model always has the final say. The win depends on draft acceptance rate and the draft model being much cheaper than the target. It is a serving-side feature, so it needs infrastructure support, but it reduces latency without changing the output distribution.

## Perceived latency as a design surface

Perceived latency is a product lever, not just an engineering one. Show a streaming cursor or a skeleton immediately so the user registers progress at TTFT. Render partial structure as it streams (headings, list items) rather than buffering until complete. Put the cheapest, most-likely-useful content first in the generation order so the earliest tokens already help. For agentic flows, stream intermediate steps (searching, reading, drafting) so a 20-second task feels like watching work rather than staring at a spinner. These do not touch total latency at all, yet they move the metric users actually report.

## Measuring it honestly

Record TTFT and total latency separately, both as distributions, and alert on p95 and p99 rather than the mean. Attribute each stage with spans (see the observability lesson): embed, search, rerank, prefill, decode, and any guardrail. A latency regression almost always lives in one stage, and without per-stage spans you are guessing. Watch the correlation between output length and total latency, because a prompt change that makes the model more verbose will raise latency with no code change and no obvious cause.

lessons.title: Fine-tune or prompt
lessons.body:
The most common senior mistake is reaching for fine-tuning first. The decision order is prompting, then retrieval, then fine-tuning, and most teams never need the last step. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can separate the three things fine-tuning actually changes, behaviour and format and latency, from the one thing it does not, which is giving the model new facts. If you say fine-tuning to add knowledge, you have failed the question.

## The decision order

```steps
Prompt | Exhaust prompting with structured outputs and few-shot examples first
Retrieve | Add RAG when the model needs facts it does not have
Fine-tune | Only when prompting plus retrieval provably cannot hit the bar
```

The order is not arbitrary. Prompting is instant to iterate and costs nothing to change. Retrieval handles private, large, or changing facts without touching the model. Fine-tuning is the slowest to iterate, creates an artifact you must host and re-train, and is the only step that cannot add fresh knowledge. So you climb the ladder only when the cheaper rung demonstrably fails.

## What fine-tuning actually changes

| Need | Right tool |
|---|---|
| New or changing facts | Retrieval, not fine-tuning |
| A consistent format or style | Fine-tuning can help |
| A narrow task at high volume, low latency | Fine-tuning can help |
| A behaviour prompting cannot reach | Fine-tuning, with evals to prove it |

Fine-tuning adjusts weights, so it teaches behaviour, tone, and output shape. It does not reliably store facts you can trust to be current, and anything it did memorize goes stale and cannot be updated without re-training. Facts belong in retrieval.

## Why fine-tuning is often a last resort

Two forces push it down the list. First, operational cost: a fine-tuned model is an artifact you host, version, monitor, and re-train. Second, base-model drift: frontier base models improve fast, and a checkpoint you tuned six months ago can end up worse than the next base release, leaving you locked to a model you now have to maintain just to keep your tuned behaviour. Chip Huyen's guidance is blunt: fine-tuning is often a last resort and many teams never do it. OpenAI's stated order reinforces it, get evaluations in place first, because you cannot rationally decide to fine-tune without the eval infrastructure to prove it helped.

> **Rule of thumb.** If you cannot measure the gap with an eval, you are not ready to fine-tune. The eval is the thing that tells you prompting plus retrieval has actually run out of road.

## A worked decision

A team wants to classify 500k support tickets per month into 40 fixed categories, with tight latency and cost limits.

```flow
dir: TB
start: 500k tickets month | actor
prompt: Prompt plus few-shot | model
evalg: Hits accuracy bar | gate
ship: Ship prompted | step
ft: Fine-tune small model | model
start -> prompt : classify
prompt -> evalg : measure
evalg -> ship : yes
evalg -> ft : no
ft -> ship : cheaper per call
```

The memo must first prove prompting-only cannot hit the accuracy bar. If it can, ship it, no fine-tuning. If it cannot, fine-tuning a small model is attractive here precisely because the task is narrow, the taxonomy is fixed, and the volume makes a cheaper per-call model pay back the training and hosting cost. This is the shape of case where fine-tuning wins: high volume, fixed taxonomy, latency and cost pressure, and a proven prompting ceiling.

## Failure modes

- Fine-tuning to add knowledge: the facts go stale and were never reliable.
- No eval: you cannot tell whether the tuned model is better or worse.
- Locking to a checkpoint: a later base model beats your tuned one and you keep maintaining it.
- Tuning before exhausting prompting: you pay the artifact cost for a gain a better prompt would have given free.

> **Interview.** State the order, name the one thing fine-tuning cannot do (add trustworthy fresh facts), and require evals before tuning. Then give the case where it wins: narrow task, fixed output space, high volume, proven prompting ceiling.

```recall
Q: Why is retrieval, not fine-tuning, the answer when the model needs new facts?
A: Fine-tuning adjusts weights and teaches behaviour and format, but any facts it memorizes are unreliable and go stale with no way to update short of re-training. Retrieval supplies current facts without touching the model.
Q: What makes base-model drift a reason to avoid fine-tuning?
A: Frontier base models improve quickly, so a checkpoint you tuned can fall behind the next base release, locking you to maintaining a model that is now worse than the stock option.
Q: Why must evals come before any fine-tuning decision?
A: Without an eval you cannot measure whether prompting plus retrieval has actually failed, nor whether the tuned model is better. The eval is what justifies climbing to the expensive rung.
Q: Describe a task where fine-tuning genuinely wins.
A: A narrow, fixed-taxonomy task at high volume with latency and cost pressure, where prompting has provably hit its ceiling, so a cheaper fine-tuned small model pays back its training and hosting cost.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Cost accounting for the ladder

Each rung has a different cost shape. Prompting cost is per-request input and output tokens, with iteration cost near zero. Retrieval adds an embedding and index cost plus the per-request tokens of the retrieved context, and its iteration cost is re-indexing. Fine-tuning adds a one-time training cost, a per-token (often lower) inference cost on the tuned model, and a recurring maintenance cost: re-training as base models move, plus hosting and monitoring an artifact. The 500k-ticket case pays back only because the recurring per-call saving, multiplied by the volume, exceeds the training plus maintenance cost. Below some volume threshold, a well-prompted frontier model is cheaper all-in despite its higher per-call price, because you pay no artifact cost.

## When fine-tuning beats a long prompt

Fine-tuning can fold a long instruction-and-examples prompt into the weights, cutting per-request input tokens. For a narrow task answered millions of times, moving 2k tokens of few-shot examples out of every prompt and into the model can dominate the economics, and the tuned small model may also beat the latency of a prompted frontier model. This is a format-and-latency win, not a knowledge win: the tuned model learns the mapping, not new facts about the world. Pair it with retrieval if the task also needs current data.

## Data and the eval gate

Fine-tuning needs clean, representative, correctly-labelled examples, and quality beats quantity: a few hundred high-quality examples often beat thousands of noisy ones, and label noise teaches the wrong mapping directly. Before tuning, freeze an eval set drawn from real traffic and never used in training, so you can compare prompted-baseline against tuned-model on the same bar. After tuning, check not only task accuracy but regressions on adjacent behaviours, since tuning on a narrow distribution can degrade general capability. The eval gate is what turns fine-tuning from a hunch into a decision you can defend. See the fine-tuning methods lesson for how SFT, LoRA, and preference optimization actually implement the training step.

lessons.title: Fine-tuning methods
lessons.body:
Once the decision to fine-tune is justified, the next question is which method. The space splits into teaching a mapping from labelled examples (supervised fine-tuning), doing it cheaply (LoRA and QLoRA), aligning to preferences (DPO and RLHF), and shrinking a model to imitate a bigger one (distillation). Interviewers probe this to see if you know what each method changes, what data it needs, and the traps: catastrophic forgetting, over-fitting a small set, and evaluating a tuned model honestly.

## Supervised fine-tuning

SFT trains the model on input-output pairs so it learns the mapping you want: given this kind of input, produce this kind of output. It is the workhorse for format, style, and narrow-task behaviour. The data is the product: a few hundred clean, representative, correctly-labelled examples usually beat thousands of noisy ones, because label noise teaches the wrong mapping directly.

```steps
Collect | Gather clean input-output pairs that represent real traffic
Split | Hold out an eval set never seen during training
Train | Minimize next-token loss on the target outputs
Evaluate | Compare against the prompted baseline on the held-out set
```

## LoRA and QLoRA

Full fine-tuning updates every weight, which is expensive to train and produces a full-size artifact per task. LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation, Hu et al., 2021) freezes the base weights and injects small trainable low-rank matrices into each layer, so you train and store only those adapters. The paper reports that for GPT-3 175B, LoRA cuts trainable parameters by about 10,000x and GPU memory by about 3x versus full fine-tuning, with no inference latency when the adapter is merged.

QLoRA (Dettmers et al., 2023) goes further: it quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit and back-propagates through it into LoRA adapters, letting you fine-tune a 65B model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit task performance.

```bars
title: LoRA vs full fine-tuning on GPT-3 175B (paper figures)
unit: x reduction
Trainable parameters | 10000
GPU memory | 3
```

Because adapters are small, you can keep many per base model and swap or even serve several at once, which is the serving story at the end of this lesson.

## Preference optimization

SFT teaches what a good answer looks like from examples. Preference optimization teaches which of two answers is better, from pairwise human (or model) comparisons, to align tone, helpfulness, and safety.

- RLHF trains a separate reward model on preference pairs, then optimizes the policy against it with reinforcement learning (typically PPO). Powerful, but a multi-stage pipeline that is hard to tune and unstable.
- DPO (Direct Preference Optimization, Rafailov et al., 2023) skips the separate reward model and the RL loop: it reparameterizes the problem so a simple classification loss on preference pairs recovers the optimal policy in closed form. The paper reports it aligns as well as or better than RLHF while being substantially simpler to implement and train.

```flow
dir: LR
pairs: Preference pairs | store
rlhf: Reward model plus RL | model
dpo: DPO classify loss | model
policy: Aligned model | model
pairs -> rlhf : two stage
pairs -> dpo : one stage
rlhf -> policy : PPO
dpo -> policy : closed form
```

## Distillation

Distillation trains a small student model to imitate a large teacher on your task distribution, using the teacher's outputs (or output distributions) as targets. It is how you turn an expensive frontier model that works into a cheap small model that is almost as good on your narrow slice. It needs production data and stable evals, so it comes last.

## Trade-offs

| Method | Teaches | Data | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| SFT | A mapping | Labelled pairs | Over-fit a small set |
| LoRA / QLoRA | Same, cheaply | Labelled pairs | Rank too low to fit the task |
| RLHF | Preferences | Pairwise comparisons | Unstable, costly pipeline |
| DPO | Preferences | Pairwise comparisons | Needs good preference data |
| Distillation | Imitate a teacher | Teacher outputs | Student ceiling below teacher |

## Failure modes

- Catastrophic forgetting: tuning hard on a narrow distribution degrades general ability the model used to have.
- Over-fitting: a tiny or unrepresentative set memorizes examples and fails on real inputs.
- Data leakage: eval examples that crept into training inflate the measured gain.
- No regression check: task accuracy rises while adjacent behaviours quietly break.

> **Interview.** Map need to method: format or narrow task is SFT (LoRA or QLoRA to make it cheap), alignment to preferences is DPO before RLHF for simplicity, shrinking a working frontier model is distillation. Then name the traps, forgetting and over-fit and leakage, and insist on a held-out eval plus a regression check.

```recall
Q: What does LoRA freeze and what does it train, and why does that help?
A: It freezes the base weights and trains only small injected low-rank matrices. That cuts trainable parameters and memory dramatically (about 10,000x fewer parameters, 3x less memory on GPT-3 175B) and lets you keep many small adapters per base model.
Q: How does DPO avoid RLHF's reward model and RL loop?
A: It reparameterizes the preference problem so a simple classification loss on preference pairs recovers the optimal policy in closed form, matching or beating RLHF while being much simpler to train.
Q: What is catastrophic forgetting and how do you catch it?
A: Fine-tuning on a narrow distribution can degrade general capability the model previously had. You catch it by evaluating adjacent and general behaviours, not just the target task, before and after tuning.
Q: Why does QLoRA matter for who can fine-tune large models?
A: It quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit and trains LoRA adapters through it, so a 65B model fits fine-tuning on a single 48GB GPU with full 16-bit task performance, bringing large-model tuning within reach of modest hardware.
Q: When is distillation the right method rather than SFT?
A: When you already have a large model that works and want a cheaper small model for a narrow slice. You train the student on the teacher's outputs, which requires production data and stable evals, so it is a late move.
```
lessons.deeper:
## The LoRA rank knob

LoRA approximates the weight update as the product of two low-rank matrices of inner dimension r. A larger r gives more capacity to fit the task but more parameters to train and store; too small an r cannot represent the needed update and underfits. A common practice is to start with a small rank (for example 8 or 16) and raise it only if the eval shows the adapter cannot capture the task. LoRA also exposes a scaling factor (often written alpha) that controls how strongly the adapter perturbs the base; it interacts with learning rate and is worth sweeping. Because the base is untouched, LoRA composes cleanly: you can merge the adapter into the weights for zero inference overhead, or keep it separate to swap tasks at serve time.

## Serving adapters

Keeping LoRA adapters separate enables multi-adapter serving: one copy of the frozen base in GPU memory, many small adapters loaded on top, routed per request. This is far cheaper than hosting a full fine-tuned model per task, and serving stacks support batching requests that use different adapters against the shared base. If instead you merge the adapter into the base, you get a single standalone model with no per-request adapter overhead but lose the swap-ability. The choice is between many-tasks-one-base (keep adapters separate) and one-task-maximum-speed (merge).

## Evaluating a tuned model

Treat evaluation as the gate, not an afterthought. Freeze a held-out set from real traffic before training and keep it out of the training data, or the measured gain is leakage. Report the prompted baseline and the tuned model on the same set so the comparison is honest. Beyond the target metric, run a regression suite on general and adjacent behaviours to catch catastrophic forgetting, and check calibration and refusal behaviour if the tuning touched safety. For preference-tuned models, pairwise human or judge comparison against the base is more informative than a single scalar score. The fine-tune-or-prompt lesson covers when to climb to this rung at all; this lesson is only about how to climb it once you are there.

lessons.title: Serving models
lessons.body:
Serving is where throughput, latency, and GPU memory collide. The engineering that makes self-hosting viable is continuous batching and paged attention, and the arithmetic that decides whether a model even fits is weights plus KV cache against GPU memory. Interviewers ask this to see whether you can size a deployment, explain why vLLM-style serving is faster, and say honestly when to self-host versus call an API.

## Continuous batching

Static batching groups a fixed set of requests, runs them together, and waits for the slowest before starting the next batch, so the GPU idles while short requests wait on a long one. Continuous batching (also called in-flight batching) instead admits and evicts requests at the token level: as soon as one request finishes a token or completes, a waiting request takes its slot. The GPU stays busy, which raises throughput sharply under mixed request lengths.

```flow
dir: LR
q: Request queue | store
sched: Scheduler | gate
gpu: GPU decode step | model
done: Finished | step
q -> sched : admit
sched -> gpu : batched step
gpu -> sched : token done
gpu -> done : sequence done
done --> sched : free slot
```

## Paged attention

The KV cache for each request grows as it generates and its final length is unknown in advance, so naive serving reserves the maximum, wasting most of it to fragmentation. PagedAttention, introduced by vLLM (Kwon et al., SOSP 2023), borrows OS virtual-memory ideas: the KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks allocated on demand and referenced through a block table, so memory is used only as sequences grow. The paper reports vLLM improves throughput by 2 to 4x at the same latency versus prior systems like FasterTransformer and Orca, with the gain larger for longer sequences.

> **Key idea.** PagedAttention removes KV-cache fragmentation so more requests fit in memory at once; continuous batching keeps the GPU busy serving them. Together they are why a modern server beats a naive one by several times.

## GPU memory arithmetic

A model fits when weights plus KV cache plus activation overhead fit in GPU memory.

Weights: parameters x bytes per parameter. A 7B model at FP16 (2 bytes) needs about 14 GB just for weights; at 4-bit (0.5 byte) about 3.5 GB.

KV cache per token: 2 (key and value) x layers x hidden size x bytes, summed per token across the batch.

```stack
title: 7B FP16 on a 24GB GPU (illustrative)
unit: GB
Weights FP16 | 14 | fixed
KV cache | 6 | grows with tokens x batch
Activations and overhead | 2
Free headroom | 2
```

The KV cache is what caps your batch size and context length: once weights are loaded, the remaining memory divided by per-token KV cost sets how many tokens-across-requests you can hold. This is the single most useful back-of-envelope in a serving interview.

## Quantization and parallelism

| Technique | Buys | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Quantization (8-bit, 4-bit) | Smaller weights, more KV room | Possible quality loss |
| Tensor parallelism | A model too big for one GPU | Inter-GPU communication |
| Continuous batching | Throughput | Scheduler complexity |
| PagedAttention | Memory efficiency, batch size | Serving stack support |

Quantization shrinks weights (and sometimes the KV cache) so a model fits a smaller GPU or leaves more room for batch; aggressive quantization can cost accuracy, so measure. Tensor parallelism splits a single model's layers across GPUs when it is too large for one, at the price of communication between them.

## Throughput versus latency

Larger batches raise throughput (tokens per second across all requests) but can raise per-request latency, because each decode step now does more work and a request may wait for a batch slot. Serving is a dial between the two: an interactive chatbot optimizes for low per-request latency with modest batches, a bulk pipeline maximizes batch size for throughput and tolerates higher per-request latency.

## When to self-host

> **Rule of thumb.** Call an API until volume, data-residency, latency floors, or a custom or fine-tuned model force self-hosting. Self-hosting trades a per-token bill for GPUs you must provision, keep busy, and operate.

Self-hosting wins when you have sustained high volume (so the GPUs stay utilized), a custom or fine-tuned model an API will not host, hard data-residency rules, or a latency floor an API cannot meet. It loses when traffic is spiky or low, because idle GPUs are pure cost, and because you now own batching, scaling, and uptime.

> **Interview.** Explain continuous batching (token-level admission keeps the GPU busy) and PagedAttention (block-allocated KV cache removes fragmentation, 2 to 4x throughput in the vLLM paper), do the weights-plus-KV memory arithmetic, then give the self-host decision rule tied to utilization.

```recall
Q: Why does continuous batching beat static batching under mixed request lengths?
A: Static batching waits for the slowest request in a batch, idling the GPU on short ones. Continuous batching admits waiting requests into freed slots at the token level, so the GPU stays busy.
Q: What problem does PagedAttention solve and what is the reported win?
A: It removes KV-cache memory fragmentation by allocating fixed-size blocks on demand instead of reserving the maximum per request, letting more requests fit. The vLLM paper reports 2 to 4x throughput at the same latency versus prior systems.
Q: A 7B FP16 model is on a 24GB GPU. What sets the maximum batch and context?
A: Weights take about 14GB fixed. The remaining memory minus activation overhead, divided by the per-token KV-cache cost, sets how many tokens across all in-flight requests you can hold.
Q: How does quantization help serving beyond just fitting the model?
A: Smaller weights free GPU memory, which can go to a larger batch (more throughput) or longer context (bigger KV cache). The risk is accuracy loss, so it must be measured.
Q: When does self-hosting beat calling an API?
A: Sustained high volume that keeps GPUs utilized, a custom or fine-tuned model an API will not serve, hard data-residency rules, or a latency floor an API cannot meet. Spiky or low traffic favors the API, since idle GPUs are wasted cost.
```
lessons.deeper:
## The KV cache formula in full

Per-token KV-cache bytes = 2 x num_layers x num_kv_heads x head_dim x bytes_per_element. The factor 2 is key and value; bytes_per_element is 2 for FP16. For a model with 32 layers, hidden size 4096, and FP16, a single token's KV cache across all layers is roughly 2 x 32 x 4096 x 2 bytes = about 512 KB per token (with full multi-head attention). Multiply by sequence length and by concurrent requests to size the cache. Grouped-query attention (GQA) and multi-query attention (MQA) shrink this by sharing key-value heads across query heads, cutting num_kv_heads and so the per-token cost, which is a major reason long-context serving is feasible. This formula, not the weights, is usually what limits how many users you can serve at once.

## Prefill and decode scheduling

A subtle serving decision is how to interleave prefill (compute-bound, processes a whole prompt at once) and decode (memory-bandwidth bound, one token per step per request). Mixing a large prefill into a batch of decodes can stall the decoders and spike their inter-token latency. Modern servers use chunked prefill, splitting a long prompt's prefill into pieces interleaved with ongoing decodes, to keep inter-token latency smooth. This is why a single very long prompt arriving can briefly degrade everyone else's streaming unless the scheduler is designed for it.

## Choosing a serving stack

vLLM popularized PagedAttention and continuous batching and is a common default for self-hosted open-weight models (verify current capabilities, as of 2026). Other stacks (TensorRT-LLM, TGI, SGLang and others) make different throughput, latency, and hardware trade-offs. The selection criteria that matter: supported quantization formats, tensor and pipeline parallelism for large models, LoRA multi-adapter serving if you ship adapters, structured-output and tool-call support, and observability hooks. Benchmark on your own request distribution, because the published throughput numbers assume request-length mixes that may not match yours. The serving lesson pairs with the latency lesson: the server decides throughput and the batching dial, while the latency lesson covers the per-request budget and streaming the server feeds.

chapters.title: The stack
chapters.summary: Frameworks, vector databases, eval tools and gateways, and what to say about them.

lessons.title: Frameworks the honest take
lessons.body:
The framework question, should we use LangChain or build on raw SDKs, is a judgment test disguised as a tooling question. A strong answer holds two true things at once instead of picking a tribe: frameworks save real work on genuinely complex control flow, and they add abstraction that obscures the prompts and responses you most need to see when debugging. Interviewers want the decision rule, not a favourite.

## The primary-sourced caution

Anthropic's engineering guidance is the anchor because it comes from a model provider, not a competing framework. In Building Effective Agents (2024) they write that many patterns can be implemented in a few lines of code, that frameworks often create extra layers of abstraction that can obscure the underlying prompts and responses, making them harder to debug, and that teams are tempted to add complexity when a simpler solution would suffice. Their top recommendation is to start with direct API calls, and if you do use a framework, to make sure you understand the underlying code.

> **Key idea.** Start with direct API calls. Reach for a framework when you hit a concrete problem it solves, not in anticipation of one.

## The landscape, by what each is for

```steps
Direct SDK | The provider client plus your own code. Maximum control and visibility, you write the loop.
Orchestration | LangChain and LlamaIndex wrap chaining, retrieval, and tool glue into reusable components.
Graph control | LangGraph models an agent as an explicit state graph for complex branching and loops.
Focused libraries | DSPy (prompt optimisation), Pydantic AI and Instructor (typed structured output).
Multi-agent | CrewAI, AutoGen, OpenAI Agents SDK, Claude Agent SDK, for coordinating several agents.
```

All of these move fast, so read their own docs rather than comparison blogs, and expect APIs to churn.

## The abstraction-leak problem

A framework earns its keep by hiding detail, but an LLM app's hardest bugs live in exactly the detail it hides: the literal prompt sent, the raw response, the token counts, the retry behaviour. When a chain misbehaves you often have to read the framework's source to see the prompt it assembled, which can cost more time than writing the twenty lines yourself. This is the recurring 2025 to 2026 practitioner complaint about LangChain specifically (convergent across independent authors, secondary): it is just a wrapper, dependency bloat, and frequent breaking changes. The sentiment went from obvious yes to it depends, and most of the time, no.

## The decision rule

```flow
dir: TB
start: New LLM project | actor
simple: Simple chain or retrieval? | gate
sdk: Direct SDK plus your code | step
complex: Complex graph control flow? | gate
graph: LangGraph or similar | step
eco: Already in an ecosystem? | gate
fw: Shared framework | step
start -> simple
simple -> sdk : yes
simple -> complex : no
complex -> graph : yes
complex -> eco : no
eco -> fw : yes
eco -> sdk : no
```

Apply it to two teams. A three-person startup prototyping with no existing investment, probably not, start with direct API calls and stay close to the metal while the product is still moving. A forty-engineer platform team standardising a dozen product teams, the case for a shared framework (consistency, tracing integration, onboarding) is real, the cost of everyone reinventing the loop differently is higher than the abstraction tax. Hold both, do not treat it as binary.

```recall
Q: What is Anthropics primary-sourced advice on frameworks, and why does the source matter?
A: Start with direct API calls, add a framework only when it clearly helps, and understand its underlying code. It matters because Anthropic is a model provider, not a competing framework, so the advice is not a sales pitch.
Q: Why do LLM frameworks cause disproportionate debugging pain?
A: The hardest bugs are in the exact prompt sent and raw response returned, which is precisely the detail a framework abstracts away, so you often must read its source to see what you need.
Q: When is a shared framework the right call despite the abstraction cost?
A: On a large multi-team org where consistency, shared tracing, and onboarding matter, the cost of everyone reinventing the loop differently exceeds the abstraction tax. A tiny prototyping team usually does not clear that bar.
Q: Why read a framework docs rather than a comparison blog?
A: These tools change fast, so comparison blogs go stale and often carry SEO or vendor bias. The primary docs reflect the current API and capabilities you will actually depend on.
Q: What does should this team use LangChain really test in an interview?
A: Judgment, whether you can weigh control and visibility against reuse and consistency and give a context-dependent rule, rather than naming a favourite tool.
```
lessons.deeper:
### What a framework actually gives you

Stripped of marketing, an orchestration framework provides four things: pre-built components (retrievers, chains, memory, tool wrappers), a standard interface so swapping a model or vector store is a config change, integrations (tracing, eval, vector DB connectors), and patterns encoded as reusable primitives. The value of each depends on scale. One developer on one app gets little from a standard interface they will never swap and integrations they could wire directly, but a platform serving many teams gets real value from a shared vocabulary and consistent tracing. This is why the honest answer is scale-dependent rather than absolute, the same abstraction that is overhead for one team is leverage for twenty.

### Graph control flow, where LangGraph earns it

The one case where a framework clearly beats hand-rolled code is genuinely complex control flow, an agent that branches, loops, retries, interrupts for human approval, and resumes from durable state. Modelling that as an explicit state graph (nodes as steps, edges as transitions, a persisted state object) is real engineering that LangGraph's primitives handle, and reimplementing it correctly, especially durable interrupt-and-resume, is substantial work. If your control flow is a straight chain or a simple retrieve-then-generate, you do not need this and the graph machinery is pure overhead, but when branching and resumable state are inherent to the problem, the primitives save weeks.

### The migration tax

A framework decision is sticky, because its abstractions spread through your code, call sites, prompt templates, memory handling, tool definitions all take the framework's shape, so leaving it later is a rewrite, not a config change. That stickiness is the real argument for starting with direct SDK calls on a young project: you keep optionality, and adopting a framework later when you understand your actual needs is far cheaper than ripping one out after it has grown into everything. The reverse migration, from a framework to raw SDKs because the abstraction got in the way, is the painful one teams report, which is itself evidence for the start-simple default.

### Focused libraries are a third option

The debate is often framed as full framework versus nothing, but focused single-purpose libraries occupy a useful middle. Instructor or Pydantic AI add typed structured outputs without taking over your control flow, DSPy optimises prompts without owning your retrieval, and you can adopt one for the one problem it solves while writing everything else directly. This composes better than a monolith, you pay abstraction cost only where it buys something, and each library is small enough to understand fully, which satisfies Anthropic's understand the underlying code caution in a way a large framework rarely does.

lessons.title: Choosing a vector database
lessons.body:
A vector database stores embeddings and answers nearest-neighbour queries fast. The interview rarely wants a product ranking, it wants the trade-off that decides between a Postgres extension, a dedicated engine, and a managed service, plus enough grasp of the index internals to reason about recall and memory. Every specific throughput, recall, or price number in this space comes from vendor or comparison-blog content, so state the shape of the trade-off confidently and re-verify any number against your own workload.

## The landscape, by category not ranking

| Option | What it is | Pitch |
|---|---|---|
| pgvector | A Postgres extension, not a standalone DB | Reuse the database you already run |
| Pinecone | Managed, hosted service | No ops, historical mindshare leader |
| Weaviate | Open-source engine | Schema flexibility, native hybrid search |
| Qdrant | Open-source, Rust | Performance focus |
| Chroma | Open-source, lightweight | Developer experience, common in prototyping |
| Milvus | Open-source, distributed | Very large scale |

## The claim that survives scrutiny

One statement recurs independently and matches sound engineering: pgvector is displacing standalone vector databases at small-to-mid scale, roughly under ten million vectors. If you already run Postgres, adding a vector column avoids standing up and operating new infrastructure, and pgvector has closed much of the performance gap at moderate scale. pgvector supports both HNSW and IVFFlat indexes, cosine, L2, and inner-product distance, and vectors up to two thousand dimensions in an index (pgvector docs, re-verify current limits).

So for a two-million-document RAG system already on Postgres, the defensible answer is add pgvector, two million is comfortably inside the cited sweet spot, while naming the roughly ten-million threshold as a heuristic to revisit with your own benchmark, not gospel.

```flow
dir: TB
need: Need vector search | actor
pg: Already run Postgres and under ~10M? | gate
addpg: Add pgvector | store
scale: Tens of millions or heavy ops? | gate
ded: Dedicated or managed engine | store
need -> pg
pg -> addpg : yes
pg -> scale : no
scale -> ded : yes
scale -> addpg : no
```

## Index internals you can reason about

The index is how the DB avoids comparing the query to every stored vector. Three ideas cover the field.

```steps
HNSW | A navigable graph of vectors. Fast and high-recall, but holds the graph in memory, so RAM cost rises with scale.
IVF | Cluster vectors into lists, search only the nearest few lists. Less memory than HNSW, recall tuned by lists probed.
PQ | Product quantization compresses each vector into a short code. Big memory savings, some recall loss from the lossy codes.
```

These compose, IVF plus PQ is common at large scale (fit more vectors in RAM via compression, prune the search space via clustering), while HNSW is the common default when memory allows because its recall is strong out of the box.

> **Numbers.** All QPS, recall-percent, pricing, and market-size figures in this space come from vendor or SEO content (illustrative at best). State the trade-off shape, HNSW trades RAM for recall, PQ trades recall for RAM, managed trades money for ops, and benchmark the specifics yourself.

## Filtered search, the operational gotcha

Real queries are rarely pure similarity, they are find similar chunks where tenant equals X and date after Y. Combining a metadata filter with ANN search is harder than it sounds: filter first and the ANN index may be bypassed, filter after and you may retrieve k results then discard most, leaving too few. How well a DB handles filtered ANN (pre-filtering, post-filtering, or integrated) is a real differentiator that a feature-list comparison hides, so it is worth testing on your actual filter patterns.

```recall
Q: Why is pgvector the defensible choice for a 2M-document RAG system on Postgres?
A: Two million is inside the under-ten-million sweet spot where pgvector competes, and reusing the existing Postgres avoids standing up and operating a separate vector service. Name the ten-million threshold as a heuristic to re-benchmark, not a hard line.
Q: What does HNSW trade for its strong recall, and why does that matter at scale?
A: Memory. It holds a navigable graph of vectors in RAM, so RAM cost grows with the corpus. At tens of millions of vectors that memory bill can force a switch to IVF or PQ compression.
Q: What problem does product quantization solve, and at what cost?
A: It compresses each vector into a short code, cutting memory sharply so far more vectors fit in RAM. The cost is some recall loss, because the codes are lossy approximations of the original vectors.
Q: Why is filtered search a real differentiator rather than a checkbox feature?
A: Combining a metadata filter with ANN is genuinely hard, filter-then-search can bypass the index and search-then-filter can leave too few results. How a DB integrates the two decides real-world quality, which a feature list hides.
Q: Why should you distrust the specific benchmark numbers in vector-DB comparisons?
A: Nearly all QPS, recall, and pricing figures come from vendor or SEO content and depend on hardware, dataset, and tuning. The trade-off shape is reliable, the exact numbers are not, so benchmark your own workload.
```
lessons.deeper:
### HNSW in a little more depth

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) builds a multi-layer graph where each vector links to a few near neighbours, with sparse long-range links in upper layers and dense local links below. A search enters at the top, greedily hops toward the query through the sparse upper layers to get close fast, then refines in the dense lower layers. Two parameters dominate: the number of neighbours per node (higher means better recall and more memory) and the search breadth (higher means better recall and slower queries). The reason it is memory-hungry is that the whole graph must be resident to traverse, so its RAM footprint scales with both vector count and the neighbour count you chose, which is the constraint that eventually pushes very large corpora toward IVF or quantization.

### IVF and the lists-probed knob

IVF (inverted file) first clusters all vectors into a set of lists using k-means, storing each vector under its nearest centroid. A query is compared to the centroids, then searched only within the few nearest lists. The tuning knob is how many lists you probe: probe one and search is fast but may miss neighbours that fell into an adjacent cluster, probe many and recall rises toward exhaustive search but you lose the speed-up. This is a direct recall-versus-latency dial, and it is why IVF indexes need their probe count tuned against an eval set rather than left at a default. pgvector exposes exactly this as its IVFFlat probes setting.

### Product quantization, concretely

PQ splits each vector into several sub-vectors and replaces each sub-vector with the id of its nearest centroid from a small per-segment codebook, so a vector that was, say, 1536 floats becomes a handful of small integer codes. Distances are then approximated from the codes, which is dramatically cheaper in memory and often in compute. The cost is approximation error: two vectors with the same codes are indistinguishable, so recall drops, and the drop grows as you compress harder. In practice PQ is combined with a reranking pass, use the compressed index to shortlist candidates cheaply, then re-score the shortlist with the full-precision vectors, recovering most of the lost recall while keeping the memory win.

### When dedicated or managed still wins

Three situations justify leaving Postgres. Very large scale, tens of millions of vectors and up, where purpose-built distributed engines (Milvus, Qdrant clusters) handle sharding and memory that pgvector would strain against. No team to own ops, where a fully managed service (Pinecone's pitch) trades money for never patching, scaling, or tuning the store yourself. And native advanced features, where an engine's built-in hybrid search or schema handling (Weaviate's pitch) saves building it on top of Postgres. The decision is the same shape as the framework decision, reuse what you run until a concrete need, scale, ops burden, or a feature, justifies the new dependency.

lessons.title: Eval tools and gateways
lessons.body:
Two stack categories, evaluation tooling and LLM gateways, are where interviewers test whether you can describe a fragmented market by its structure rather than by reciting whichever products a blog ranked this month. The useful knowledge is the taxonomy and what each layer buys you, because the specific product names churn and the capabilities overlap. Verify current names and features against primary docs, this lesson gives you the map, not a frozen ranking.

## Eval tools: a fragmented category, honestly

The eval-tool space is genuinely fragmented, and saying so is the honest state. Names you will hear: RAGAS (RAG-specific metrics), DeepEval (broad open-source), LangSmith (coupled to LangChain), Braintrust (evaluation-first commercial), Arize Phoenix (open-source, framework-agnostic), Langfuse (open-source, self-hostable), OpenAI Evals (first-party). The list is not the answer, the taxonomy is.

| Axis | One end | Other end |
|---|---|---|
| Licence | Open-source, self-host | Commercial, hosted |
| Granularity | Trajectory, did the agent take a good path | Final output only |
| Mode | Offline, run experiments | Online, monitor production |
| Coupling | Framework-coupled | Framework-agnostic |

That mental model is sound regardless of which post you read, and it is what lets you place a new tool the moment you hear its pitch.

## Gateways: one endpoint in front of many providers

An LLM gateway (or router) is a proxy that sits between your application and the model providers, exposing one endpoint that routes to many models. It becomes worth adding the moment you call more than one provider or want to swap providers without rewriting call sites.

```flow
dir: LR
app: Application | actor
gw: LLM gateway | gate
pa: Provider A | model
pb: Provider B | model
cache: Cache | store
log: Cost and logs | store
app -> gw : one endpoint
gw -> pa : route or fallback
gw --> pb : fallback
gw -> cache : read and write
gw -> log : usage
```

What a gateway buys you: routing (pick a model per request), fallback (retry another provider when one fails or is down), caching (reuse repeated calls), budgets (per-key and per-tenant spend limits), and centralised logs (one place for cost and latency across providers). The named options recur consistently: LiteLLM (open-source, self-hosted, no per-token markup) for teams willing to operate it, OpenRouter (managed, zero-setup, many models), Portkey (managed, enterprise governance). All fast-moving, verify current capabilities.

> **Key idea.** A gateway turns provider choice into a config decision instead of a code change, which is what makes model routing, fallback, and cost governance possible without touching call sites.

## The trend worth naming

A directional, secondary-sourced trend: gateways are evolving from a 2024 convenience toward the control point of the AI stack. Cost governance, guardrails, and compliance increasingly sit at the gateway layer rather than scattered through application code, because the gateway is the one place every model call already passes through. Multiple 2026 references frame it this way (secondary, convergent, re-verify), and the architectural logic is sound, a single choke point is the natural home for cross-cutting policy.

```recall
Q: Why describe eval tools by a taxonomy instead of a ranked list?
A: The market is fragmented and the products churn, so a ranking goes stale and carries vendor bias. The axes, open vs commercial, trajectory vs output, offline vs online, coupled vs agnostic, let you place any tool from its pitch and stay current.
Q: At what point does an LLM gateway start to pay for itself?
A: As soon as you call more than one provider or want to swap providers without rewriting call sites. It centralises routing, fallback, caching, budgets, and logs that would otherwise be scattered per call site.
Q: What specifically does fallback in a gateway protect against?
A: A provider outage, rate limit, or error on one model, the gateway retries the request against another provider or model so a single provider failure does not take down your feature.
Q: What does it mean to call the gateway the control point of the stack?
A: Every model call passes through it, so it is the natural place to enforce cross-cutting policy, cost budgets, guardrails, and compliance, rather than duplicating that logic across application code.
Q: Why distinguish trajectory-level from final-output eval for agents?
A: An agent can reach a correct answer through a wrong or wasteful path, or a right path that happened to fail. Trajectory eval judges the steps taken, output eval judges only the end result, and agents need both.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why the eval market is so fragmented

Evaluation spans jobs that are genuinely different, so no single tool dominates. RAG evaluation needs retrieval metrics (recall at k, mean reciprocal rank) and generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance), which is why RAG-specific tools exist. Agent evaluation needs trajectory analysis, did the agent pick good tools in a sensible order, which is a different data shape entirely. Production monitoring needs online capture of real traffic with feedback loops, while development needs offline experiment-running against fixed datasets. A tool optimised for one of these is awkward at another, so teams often run two, one for offline experiments and one for online monitoring, and the taxonomy axes are really a map of which job each tool was built for.

### What a gateway does not solve

A gateway centralises calls, but it does not make a bad model choice good, nor does it fix a prompt or a retrieval defect, it operates below the quality layer. It also adds a hop, so it introduces its own latency (small, often single-digit milliseconds for a thin proxy, but non-zero) and its own failure mode, if the gateway is down, everything behind it is unreachable, which is why self-hosted gateways need the same reliability engineering as any critical infrastructure. And a semantic cache in a gateway, returning a stored answer for a similar-enough query, carries a real correctness risk: two questions that embed close together can have different correct answers, so semantic caching trades accuracy for cost and must be scoped carefully. The gateway is plumbing, powerful plumbing, but not a substitute for the quality work upstream of it.

### How the two categories connect

Eval tools and gateways meet in production. The gateway is where every call is logged, so it is the natural source of the traffic that feeds online evaluation and the dataset you build offline evals from, real production inputs are the best eval data. Several tools blur the line deliberately, offering both tracing or gateway features and evaluation in one product, which is convenient but re-raises the coupling question, a combined tool that is excellent at gateway duties may be mediocre at eval, or lock you into one vendor for both. The principle-first answer is to keep the layers conceptually separate, know what routing, logging, and evaluation each require, so you can judge whether a bundled product actually serves all of them or just one well.

### Keeping the answer current

Every product name here is a moving target, licences change, companies get acquired, capabilities expand, so the durable skill is the structure, not the roster. In an interview, lead with the taxonomy and the capability list (routing, fallback, caching, budgets, logs for gateways, the four axes for eval), name a representative example or two with the caveat that the space moves fast, and say you would verify current features against primary docs before committing. That demonstrates exactly the signal-from-hype judgment the question is testing, which outlasts any specific tool.

lessons.title: What to say about the stack
lessons.body:
Most search results for best X in 2026 are SEO or vendor content with suspiciously precise, unverifiable numbers, dozens of near-identical posts. The question an interviewer is really asking when they probe your stack is not which tools do you like, it is can you tell signal from hype. The strongest answer demonstrates that judgment: lead with what has primary backing, flag what is marketing, and show you decide by benchmarking your own workload, not by a blog's ranking.

## Three moves that show judgment

```steps
Name the consensus | State the claims with primary backing from providers or papers, and attribute them.
Flag the hype | Call out best-tool-in-2026 rankings as vendor or SEO content to benchmark, not trust.
Show the test | Say how you would decide, your own eval set and workload, not someone elses leaderboard.
```

### Primary-backed claims to anchor on

- Start with direct API calls before a framework, Anthropic's own advice in Building Effective Agents.
- Prompt caching and model routing are proven cost levers with hard numbers from the providers themselves.
- RAG versus long context is a real, actively researched trade-off, not settled.
- LLM-as-judge has documented, paper-backed bias problems (position, verbosity, self-preference) you design around.
- Contextual retrieval cut retrieval failures by measured amounts in Anthropic's published tests.

These share a property: a named primary source stands behind each, so you can state them with confidence and say where they come from.

### What is hype-adjacent

Most best vector DB, best gateway, best eval tool in 2026 rankings are vendor or SEO content. The numbers in them, QPS, recall percent, pricing, market size, are precise, unsourced, and mutually contradictory across posts. A good engineer treats them as leads to verify, not facts to repeat.

## Signal versus hype, side by side

| Claim type | How to treat it | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Primary-sourced | State confidently, cite the source | Anthropic measured 49 to 67 percent fewer retrieval failures |
| Provider pricing mechanic | Reason in ratios, re-verify | Cache reads cost a fraction of fresh input |
| Vendor or SEO ranking | Benchmark yourself, do not quote | Best vector database of 2026 |
| Unsourced precise number | Distrust until verified | This gateway adds exactly 3.2 ms |

> **Interview.** The question best X in 2026 is a trap for the overconfident. The strong answer names the primary-backed consensus, labels the rest as benchmark-it-yourself, and describes the test you would run. That judgment is the thing being graded, more than any tool name.

## A minimal defensible stack

When asked to pick, do not reach for the longest tool list, reach for the smallest stack that meets the need and name why each piece is there: a model behind a thin gateway (routing, fallback, cost logs), retrieval if the data is private or fresh (Postgres with pgvector until scale forces more), an eval set from day one, and tracing so you can see what happened. Add nothing until a concrete problem demands it. This mirrors the start-simple default that runs through the whole stack.

```recall
Q: What is an interviewer really testing with a best tool in 2026 question?
A: Whether you can separate signal from hype, not which tool you prefer. The graded skill is knowing which claims have primary backing and which are vendor or SEO content.
Q: What property do the trustworthy stack claims share?
A: A named primary source stands behind each, a provider's own guidance, published measurements, or a paper, so you can state it confidently and attribute it, rather than repeating an unsourced number.
Q: How should you treat a precise, unsourced number from a comparison blog?
A: Distrust it until verified. Precision without a source, especially one that contradicts other posts, is a hype signal, treat it as a lead to benchmark on your own workload, not a fact.
Q: What does a minimal defensible stack look like, and why minimal?
A: Model behind a thin gateway, retrieval only if data is private or fresh, an eval set from day one, tracing. Minimal because every added tool is cost and complexity you must justify by a concrete need, matching the start-simple default.
Q: Why re-check anything version- or number-specific in this area?
A: The field moves fast, prices, capabilities, and tool names change within months, so a specific figure true today can be stale by the time you rely on it. State the trade-off shape, re-verify the specifics.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why precise numbers are a hype tell

A genuine measurement comes with its conditions, which hardware, which dataset, which model version, which tuning, because the number is meaningless without them. SEO and vendor content strips those conditions and presents a bare figure, this DB does fifty thousand QPS, because the goal is persuasion, not reproduction. So precision without conditions is itself the signal to distrust: the more exact and the less sourced a number is, the more likely it was chosen to impress rather than measured to inform. The habit to build is to ask, of any number, where was this measured and under what conditions, and to treat a figure that cannot answer that as decorative.

### Principle-first beats tool-first

The reason to lead with principles rather than tools is that principles outlast the roster. Start simple, measure before tuning, retrieval before generation, prompt before fine-tune, keep cross-cutting policy at a choke point, these have held across several generations of tooling and will survive the next. A tool-first answer dates immediately, the moment the named product is superseded, acquired, or renamed, the answer is stale. A principle-first answer stays correct and lets you place any new tool against a stable frame. In an interview this reads as seniority, because it is exactly how an experienced engineer evaluates something they have not seen before.

### Build versus buy, decided by principle

The stack is full of build-or-buy decisions, framework or SDK, managed or self-hosted vector DB, gateway service or your own proxy, and they resolve to one rule: reuse what you already run and buy ops you do not want to own, until a concrete need, scale, a feature, a compliance requirement, justifies the new dependency. The failure mode in both directions is anticipatory, building infrastructure for scale you do not have, or buying a platform for complexity you have not hit. The discipline is to let a real, present problem pull each decision, which keeps the stack minimal and every component justifiable, and that justifiability is what a design interview is probing when it asks you to defend your choices.

### A decision checklist

For any stack component, five questions settle it. What concrete problem does this solve that I have right now? Is the claim behind it primary-sourced or marketing? What is the simplest thing that could work instead? How would I benchmark it on my own workload? And what does adopting it cost me in complexity, lock-in, and ops? Running a proposed tool through those five, out loud, is both how you make the decision in practice and how you demonstrate the judgment the interview is testing, it turns best X in 2026 from a quiz you can fail into a reasoning process you can show.

chapters.title: Design cases
chapters.summary: Three worked system designs and a framework for any AI design question.

lessons.title: Design a support assistant
lessons.body:
A customer-support assistant is the most common AI design question because it touches everything: retrieval, generation, guardrails, human handoff, evals, and cost, all under a real quality bar where a wrong answer has consequences. The interviewer wants to see you clarify requirements first, then walk the request path end to end, then name the failure modes and how you would measure them. This lesson is a worked architecture, not a checklist to recite.

## Clarify first

Before any design, pin down the shape of the problem.

- Scope: deflect common questions, or also take actions (refunds, order changes)?
- Knowledge: how large is the help content, how often does it change, is any of it per-user?
- Stakes: what is the cost of a confidently wrong answer, and what must never be automated?
- Volume and latency: how many conversations, and what response-time expectation?
- Handoff: is there a human support team to escalate to, and how?

The answers decide almost everything downstream. A read-only FAQ deflector and an agent that can issue refunds are different systems with different risk.

## Architecture

```flow
dir: LR
user: Customer | actor
guard: Input guard | gate
retr: Retrieve docs | store
llm: Generate answer | model
cite: Check citations | gate
human: Human agent | actor
user -> guard : question
guard -> retr : query
retr -> llm : top-k chunks
llm -> cite : draft plus sources
cite -> user : grounded answer
cite --> human : low confidence
guard --> human : out of scope
```

The spine is RAG: retrieve relevant help content, generate an answer grounded in it, and cite sources. Two gates bracket the model: an input guard screens scope and safety, and a citation check gates the output. Both can route to a human.

## The request path

```steps
Ingest | Chunk and embed help docs offline, re-index on content change
Guard input | Screen for abuse, out-of-scope, and account-specific requests
Retrieve | Hybrid search plus rerank over the help index, scoped by product
Generate | Answer only from retrieved context, with inline citations
Verify | Check the answer is grounded in sources and confident enough
Handoff | Escalate low-confidence, action-requiring, or angry conversations to a human
```

The non-negotiable rule: the model answers from retrieved context and cites it, so a reviewer can trace every claim. If retrieval returns nothing relevant, the bot says it does not know and offers a human, rather than inventing an answer.

## Guardrails and handoff

| Risk | Guardrail |
|---|---|
| Abuse, prompt injection | Input classifier, isolate user text from instructions |
| Hallucinated answer | Require citations, verify grounding, refuse if unsupported |
| Out-of-scope or sensitive | Route to human, do not answer |
| Taking a risky action | Human approval before any state change |

Handoff is a feature, not a failure. The strong design escalates on low retrieval confidence, on any request that would change account state, and on detected frustration, carrying the conversation context to the human so the customer does not repeat themselves.

> **Pitfall.** A support bot that always produces an answer is worse than one that sometimes says I do not know and hands off. Confident wrong answers in support erode trust and create liability.

## Evals

Build the eval set from real tickets before launch and keep it fresh from production.

- Retrieval: recall@k on a labelled set of question-to-correct-doc pairs. Measure this first; generation cannot fix missing context.
- Generation: faithfulness (is every claim supported by sources), answer relevance, and citation correctness.
- End to end: resolution rate, escalation rate, and a sampled human review of a slice of live conversations.

Gate releases on these in CI so a prompt or index change cannot silently regress quality.

## Cost and latency

Cost per conversation is dominated by retrieved-context tokens and output length; cache the stable system prompt and tool schemas, and keep retrieved context tight. Latency is TTFT plus retrieval plus generation; stream the answer so the customer sees it immediately. For a high-volume deflection bot, route simple FAQ hits to a small model and reserve a frontier model for complex multi-part questions.
