> **Interview.** Lead with clarifying questions (actions or read-only, stakes, handoff), draw the RAG spine with input and output gates, make grounded-with-citations the hard rule, treat handoff as a designed path, and name the metric per stage: recall@k for retrieval, faithfulness for generation, resolution and escalation end to end.

```recall
Q: Why is handoff a core feature of a support assistant rather than an edge case?
A: Confident wrong answers in support erode trust and create liability. Escalating low-confidence, action-requiring, and frustrated conversations to a human, with context carried over, is safer than always answering.
Q: What is the non-negotiable generation rule and why?
A: The model answers only from retrieved context and cites sources, so every claim is traceable. If retrieval finds nothing relevant, it says it does not know rather than inventing an answer.
Q: Why measure retrieval recall@k before generation metrics?
A: Generation cannot recover context that retrieval failed to surface. If the right document is not in the top-k, no amount of prompt tuning fixes the answer, so retrieval quality is the first gate.
Q: How does letting the bot take actions change the design?
A: Any state-changing action (refund, order change) needs a human-approval gate and tighter guardrails, because the cost of an error jumps from a wrong answer to a wrong transaction. A read-only deflector does not carry that risk.
Q: Where does cost per conversation mostly go, and how do you cut it?
A: Mostly retrieved-context tokens and output length. Cache the stable system prompt and tool schemas, keep retrieved context tight, and route simple FAQ questions to a small model while reserving the frontier model for hard ones.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Ingestion and freshness

Help content changes, so ingestion is a pipeline, not a one-time load. Chunk documents structurally (by section, preserving headings as metadata), embed with the same model used for queries, and index with metadata for product, locale, and version so retrieval can filter. When a doc changes, re-embed and re-index just that document; a full re-index on every edit is wasteful and slow. Stale content is a silent failure: the bot confidently cites a policy that changed last week. Track content age and surface it, and consider a freshness signal in retrieval so newer authoritative docs win ties.

## The confidence signal for handoff

The escalation decision needs a usable confidence signal, and there are several, best combined. Retrieval score: if the top chunks are far from the query in embedding space, context is weak. Grounding check: run a lightweight judge or a self-consistency check asking whether the drafted answer is fully supported by the cited sources, and escalate if not. Intent and sentiment: a classifier on the user turn catches explicit requests for a human and detected frustration. Action detection: any request that maps to a state-changing tool routes to approval. Calibrate the thresholds against a labelled set of should-have-escalated conversations, and watch the escalation rate as an operating metric, because approval fatigue cuts both ways: too much escalation overwhelms the human team, too little lets bad answers through.

## Measuring resolution honestly

Resolution rate is the headline business metric but is easy to game. A conversation that ends is not necessarily resolved; the customer may have given up. Pair automated resolution (the conversation closed without escalation) with a sampled human review and, where possible, a follow-up signal (did the customer re-open a ticket on the same issue within a few days). Slice every metric by topic and by product, because an aggregate resolution rate can hide a category where the bot is systematically wrong. Feed reviewed failures back into the eval set so the golden set tracks real production weaknesses rather than the questions you imagined at launch. The RAG, guardrails, and evals lessons go deeper on each stage; this case is about wiring them into one system under a real quality bar.

lessons.title: Design a coding agent
lessons.body:
A coding agent is the canonical agent design question because it exercises every part of the stack at once: a tool set, an autonomous loop, context management over a long task, real evals, and safety around actions that change a live codebase. The interviewer is not testing whether you can describe an agent; they are testing whether you reach for autonomy only where it is earned and whether you can name how the system fails. Work through requirements, tools and sandbox, the loop, context, evals, safety, and cost, in that order.

## Requirements

Pin the scope before designing. A coding agent that resolves a described issue in an existing repository has concrete requirements: read the issue, locate the relevant code, make a change, verify it with the test suite, and produce a patch, without breaking unrelated code or touching things it was not asked to. The acceptance signal is objective, the existing tests that were failing now pass and the ones that passed still pass, which is exactly how SWE-bench scores a run (2,294 real GitHub issue and pull-request pairs from 12 Python repositories; Jimenez et al., 2023). That objective signal is what makes coding a good agent domain: the environment grades the work.

## Tools and sandbox

The tool set is the agent-computer interface; keep it small and orthogonal.

| Tool | Risk tier | Policy |
|---|---|---|
| read_file, search | Read-only | Run freely |
| run_tests | Reversible (sandboxed) | Run freely |
| apply_patch | Reversible with undo | Run freely in sandbox, gated to prod |
| run_command | Varies by command | Sandboxed; gate network and destructive |
| open_pr, push | External | Require approval |

Everything runs in a sandbox: an isolated checkout with no network by default and no access to production credentials. The sandbox is what lets read, edit, and test run freely, because a mistake is contained to a throwaway environment. A run_tests tool must return the failing assertion and line, not just pass or fail, so the model can act on the error directly rather than guess.

## The architecture

```flow
dir: TB
issue: Issue text | actor
loop: Agent loop | model
search: Search and read | tool
edit: Apply patch | tool
test: Run tests | tool
cap: Caps and gate | gate
pr: Open PR | gate
issue -> loop : task
loop -> search : locate code
search -> loop : files and context
loop -> edit : change
edit -> test : verify
test -> loop : failures as observations
loop -> cap : propose next step
cap -> loop : under budget, continue
cap -> pr : tests green, request approval
```

The loop is plan, act, observe, adjust: locate the code, read it, edit, run tests, read failures, re-plan. Failures return as observations so the model corrects itself. The cap-and-gate node enforces a max-iteration count and a cost budget on every step, and routes the final patch to a human approval before any PR or push.

## Context management

A real repository does not fit in the window, and a multi-file change can run dozens of iterations, so context engineering is central. Use just-in-time retrieval: hand the agent search and read tools rather than the whole codebase, and let it pull only the files a step needs. Protect working state, the issue, the plan, the files currently open, the failing tests, and compact the loop history when it nears the limit, keeping decisions and open failures while dropping stale tool output. For a very large task, a sub-agent can explore a subsystem in an isolated window and return a digest, keeping the lead's context small.

## Evals

Two layers. A SWE-bench-style end-to-end eval scores whether the agent's patch makes the previously failing tests pass on a held-out set of real issues; this is the outcome metric. Your own evals cover what the public benchmark does not: your repositories, your languages, your common issue types, plus regressions you have seen the agent cause. Gate changes to the agent (prompt, tools, model) behind these evals in CI, so a tweak that helps one case but breaks three is caught before it ships. Measure not just resolve rate but also cost per resolved issue and the rate of unrequested changes.

## Safety and approvals

Gate on blast radius. Read and sandboxed test runs are free; applying a patch inside the sandbox is reversible; opening a PR, pushing, or running a networked command is external and requires human approval. The sandbox plus the caps plus the approval gate are three independent containments: the sandbox limits where damage can reach, the caps limit how long a confused loop runs, and the gate puts a human in front of anything that escapes the sandbox.

> **Pitfall.** Letting the agent push or open a PR without a human reviewing the diff. The tests passing does not mean the change is correct or scoped; a patch can make tests green by deleting the test or by a change far broader than the issue. The approval gate must show the exact diff.

> **Interview.** The strong design names the objective signal (tests the environment grades), keeps the tool set small with rich error returns, contains everything in a sandbox, caps the loop, gates external actions, and evals on your own repos, not just the public benchmark.

## Failure modes

| Failure | Cause | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Thrashing loop | No stop condition, poor error returns | Max-iteration and cost caps; return assertion and line |
| Context rot | Loop history fills the window | Compaction, just-in-time retrieval, protect working state |
| Tests gamed | Change passes by editing or deleting tests | Freeze the test files; human reviews the diff |
| Scope creep | Patch touches unrelated code | Measure unrequested-change rate; approval gate |
| Sandbox escape | Networked or credentialed command | No network and no prod creds by default; gate run_command |

```recall
Q: Why is a coding agent a good domain for autonomy?
A: The environment supplies an objective grade: the previously failing tests pass and the passing ones still pass. That lets the agent verify its own work in a loop instead of relying on a model to judge correctness.
Q: What three independent containments keep a coding agent safe?
A: A sandbox (limits where damage reaches), caps on iterations and cost (limit how long a confused loop runs), and a human approval gate on external actions (reviews anything leaving the sandbox).
Q: Why eval on your own repositories and not just SWE-bench?
A: SWE-bench covers specific public Python repos and issue types. Your evals cover your languages, repos, common issues, and regressions you have observed, and gate agent changes in CI so a tweak that helps one case but breaks others is caught.
Q: How can passing tests still be a failure?
A: The agent can game the tests by editing or deleting them, or make a change far broader than the issue that happens to keep tests green. Freeze test files and have a human review the exact diff before any PR.
```
lessons.deeper:
### Why the test suite is the design keystone

Most agent domains lack a cheap, objective verifier, which is why they lean on an LLM judge and inherit its bias. A codebase ships its own verifier: the test suite. This single fact reshapes the whole design. The loop can run act-observe tightly because run_tests gives ground truth each iteration; the eval is objective because the environment grades the patch; and the safety story has a sharp edge because "tests pass" is checkable. The catch is that the verifier is only as good as the tests, which is why gaming the tests (deleting a failing test, over-fitting to it) is the signature coding-agent failure and why the test files are frozen and the diff is human-reviewed. A design that treats the test suite as the keystone, and names its limits, is the one that reads as senior.

### Context over a long task, concretely

An issue touching four files across a 200k-line repository cannot pre-load the code, so the agent navigates like a developer: grep for a symbol, open the file the match points to, read the surrounding function, follow a call. This is just-in-time retrieval, and it keeps the window on the few files that matter instead of the whole tree. As the loop runs long, history accumulates: twenty tool results, several failed edits, the running plan. Near the limit the agent compacts, writing "changed the auth signature in modules A and B; test_login still failing on the token path; config.ts is off-limits" and restarting from that plus the open files. Without this the earliest instruction gets buried and the agent regresses on something it already got right.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Agent
    participant R as Repo (sandbox)
    participant T as Tests
    participant H as Human
    A->>R: search and read, apply patch
    A->>T: run tests
    T-->>A: failing assertion and line
    Note over A: re-plan, caps enforced
    A->>H: tests green, review diff
    H-->>A: approve, open PR
```

### Cost shape

Cost is dominated by the loop length and the context carried each step, not by the one final answer. A task that converges in five tight iterations with a small working set is cheap; one that thrashes for forty iterations with a bloating window is expensive and more likely to fail, so cost and reliability move together. The levers are the same ones that improve correctness: better tool returns (fewer wasted iterations), aggressive context curation (smaller per-step cost), and tight caps (a hard ceiling on a runaway). Measure cost per resolved issue, not cost per call, because the number that matters is what a correct outcome costs end to end.

### Source and currency

The objective-grading setup, 2,294 real GitHub issue and pull-request pairs across 12 Python repositories, and the fail-to-pass scoring are from the SWE-bench paper (Jimenez et al., "Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?", 2023); SWE-bench Verified is a human-vetted subset. The tool, loop, context, and safety design draws on Anthropic's agent-building guidance. Benchmark numbers and agent harnesses move fast as of 2026, so cite the benchmark structure as stable and treat any resolve-rate figure as a snapshot to re-check.

lessons.title: Design document extraction at scale
lessons.body:
Extracting structured data from documents at scale (invoices, contracts, forms) is a design question that rewards engineering judgment over model cleverness. The hard parts are not the prompt: they are batch versus online processing, enforcing a schema, scoring confidence, and routing low-confidence results to a human review queue. The interviewer wants a pipeline that is cheap, correct where it is confident, and safe where it is not.

## Clarify first

- Volume and latency: millions of docs overnight, or a few per second interactively?
- Document variety: a fixed template, or arbitrary layouts and languages?
- Schema: what fields, which are required, what types and constraints?
- Error tolerance: what is the cost of a wrong field versus a missed one?
- Review capacity: how many documents can humans check per day?

These set the batch-versus-online choice and the confidence threshold for review.

## Batch versus online

| Mode | When | Lever |
|---|---|---|
| Batch | Large backlogs, no human waiting | Batch API at reduced cost, high throughput |
| Online | Per-document, user is waiting | Low latency, stream status |

Most extraction-at-scale work is batch: documents arrive in bulk and nobody is blocked on a single one, so you use an asynchronous batch API at a discount and optimize for throughput. Reserve online processing for the interactive cases where a user uploads one document and waits.

## Architecture

```flow
dir: LR
doc: Document | actor
prep: Parse and OCR | step
llm: Extract to schema | model
val: Validate schema | gate
conf: Confidence check | gate
store: Store record | store
review: Review queue | actor
doc -> prep : raw file
prep -> llm : text plus layout
llm -> val : candidate fields
val -> conf : typed record
conf -> store : high confidence
conf --> review : low confidence
review -> store : corrected
```

Parse and OCR turn the file into text (and layout, which matters for forms). The model extracts fields into a schema. A validator enforces types and required fields. A confidence gate decides: store directly, or send to a human review queue. Corrected records flow back to storage and, ideally, into the eval set.

## Structured outputs and validation

The extraction must emit a typed record, not prose, so use schema-constrained decoding (or JSON mode) and validate every result against the schema.

```steps
Constrain | Decode against the field schema so the output is parseable
Validate | Check required fields, types, enums, and value ranges
Repair | On a validation failure, retry once with the error fed back
Confidence | Score each field and the record for the review decision
Route | Store high-confidence records, queue low-confidence for review
```

Validation catches the structural failures (missing field, wrong type, enum drift, truncation). It does not catch a well-formed but wrong value, which is what the confidence score and the review queue are for.

## The confidence and review queue

The review queue is the safety mechanism that lets you automate most volume without accepting silent errors.

> **Key idea.** You do not need the model to be right every time, only to know when it is unsure. A good confidence signal plus a human queue converts an imperfect extractor into a reliable pipeline.

Set the threshold from the error tolerance and the review capacity: a lower threshold sends more to humans (safer, more expensive), a higher one automates more (cheaper, riskier). Track the queue rate as an operating metric and the review correction rate as a quality signal, since a rising correction rate on auto-accepted records means the threshold is too loose.

## Evals and cost

- Field-level accuracy on a labelled set, sliced by field and document type, because an aggregate hides a field that is systematically wrong.
- Precision and recall per field: a missed field and a wrong field often have different costs.
- Auto-accept rate and review correction rate as the operating pair.

Cost is dominated by input tokens (document length) times volume; batch pricing and tight prompts matter most. Human review is a real cost line, so the confidence threshold is a cost-versus-risk dial, not just a quality knob.

> **Interview.** Choose batch for bulk (asynchronous, discounted), make the output schema-constrained and validated with a repair retry, add a confidence score feeding a human review queue, and set the threshold from error tolerance against review capacity. Slice field accuracy, and treat review as a designed path, not a failure.

```recall
Q: Why is batch processing usually right for extraction at scale?
A: Documents arrive in bulk and no human is waiting on a single one, so an asynchronous batch API at a discount and optimized for throughput fits, rather than paying for low latency nobody needs.
Q: What does schema validation catch, and what does it miss?
A: It catches structural failures (missing or wrong-typed fields, enum drift, truncation). It misses a well-formed but factually wrong value, which is why you also need a confidence score and a human review queue.
Q: How do you set the confidence threshold for the review queue?
A: From the error tolerance and the review capacity. Lower threshold routes more to humans (safer, costlier), higher automates more (cheaper, riskier). Track auto-accept rate and review correction rate to tune it.
Q: Why slice field-level accuracy instead of reporting one number?
A: An aggregate accuracy can hide a single field that is systematically extracted wrong. Slicing by field and document type surfaces the weak spots that an overall score masks.
Q: What is the repair step and when does it fire?
A: On a schema-validation failure, retry the extraction once with the validation error fed back to the model, so it can fix a malformed output before the record goes to the confidence gate.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Confidence signals for extraction

Extraction confidence can come from several sources, best combined. Token-level logprobs over the extracted span give a rough per-field confidence, usable but poorly calibrated alone. Self-consistency, running extraction two or three times (or at a low temperature) and checking agreement, flags unstable fields: disagreement is a strong uncertainty signal. Cross-field validation uses domain constraints (line items summing to a total, a date within a plausible range, a tax rate matching a jurisdiction) to catch values that are individually plausible but mutually inconsistent. Source grounding checks that an extracted value actually appears in the document text, catching invented fields. Combine these into a per-field score and a record-level score, calibrate against a labelled set, and route to review on the record score so one shaky field pulls the whole document to a human.

## Why layout and OCR dominate quality

For scanned forms and invoices, the ceiling on extraction accuracy is usually set before the model sees anything, by OCR and layout parsing. A number misread by OCR is wrong no matter how good the extractor, and a model given a flat text dump of a two-column form loses the spatial relationships that disambiguate which label a value belongs to. Preserve layout: pass bounding boxes or a structured representation, keep table structure, and feed the model positional context. Measure OCR quality separately from extraction quality, because conflating them hides the real bottleneck. For high-stakes fields, a hybrid of deterministic parsing (regex or template matching where the layout is fixed) and model extraction (for the variable parts) often beats model-only.

## Operating the queue over time

The review queue is a feedback loop, not just a safety net. Every human correction is a labelled example: feed it back into the eval set so the golden set tracks real production errors, and use accumulated corrections to decide whether to fine-tune a smaller model (see the fine-tune-or-prompt lesson) once volume and a stable schema justify it. Monitor the auto-accept rate and the correction rate on audited auto-accepted records together: if correction rate on audits rises, the threshold has drifted loose relative to a changing document distribution, and you tighten it. Watch for distribution shift, a new vendor's invoice format or a new document type, which shows up as a spike in queue rate for a slice, and handle it with new eval examples rather than loosening the threshold to clear the backlog.

lessons.title: A framework for AI design questions
lessons.body:
AI design questions are open-ended on purpose, and interviewers are grading your process more than your final diagram. A repeatable framework keeps you from jumping to an architecture before you understand the problem, which is the single most common failure. The order is clarify, data, model, architecture, eval, cost and latency, risks. This lesson gives a checklist for each step and a short worked example so the structure is concrete.

## The seven steps

```steps
Clarify | Pin scope, stakes, volume, latency, and what must not be automated
Data | What knowledge, where it lives, how it changes, who may see it
Model | Capability tier, context size, the latency price quality triangle
Architecture | The request path: retrieval, generation, tools, gates
Eval | How you measure quality per stage, before and after launch
Cost and latency | Per-request budget and the levers to hit it
Risks | Failure modes, guardrails, and human checkpoints
```

Do them roughly in order, but loop back: a cost constraint can change the model, a risk can change the architecture. The discipline is to not skip clarify and data, which is where weak candidates lose the most points.

## Clarify

State the problem back and ask the questions that change the design: read-only or action-taking, stakes of a wrong answer, volume and latency expectations, and what must stay human. Narrow the scope explicitly; a smaller well-defined system beats a vague ambitious one.

## Data

Most AI systems live or die on data. Ask what knowledge the system needs, whether it is private, large, or changing, how fresh it must be, and who is allowed to see what. The answers decide retrieval versus fine-tuning versus long context, and surface permissions and freshness constraints early.

## Model

Pick a capability tier, not a brand. Reasoning task, or simple extraction? Does it need a large context? Then place it on the latency, price, quality triangle: you optimize two at the expense of the third. Say you would select by eval, not by leaderboard, and would wire a fallback.

## Architecture

Draw the request path.

```flow
dir: LR
user: User | actor
guard: Input gate | gate
retr: Retrieve | store
model: Generate | model
check: Output gate | gate
user -> guard : request
guard -> retr : query
retr -> model : context
model -> check : draft
check -> user : response
```

Keep components swappable and name why each exists. Gates bracket the model; retrieval grounds it; tools let it act. Prefer the simplest shape that meets the bar: a workflow before an agent, prompting before fine-tuning.

## Eval, cost and latency, risks

- Eval: name the metric per stage (recall@k for retrieval, faithfulness for generation, task accuracy end to end) and say you gate releases on them. Evals come first, not last.
- Cost and latency: give a per-request budget, split it, and name the lever per stage (caching, routing, smaller model, streaming).
- Risks: list concrete failure modes (hallucination, injection, stale data, runaway cost) and the guardrail or human checkpoint for each.

> **Pitfall.** Drawing boxes before clarifying scope and data. An architecture that answers the wrong problem, however elegant, fails the question.

## A worked mini-example

Prompt: design a system to answer policy questions for employees.

- Clarify: read-only Q&A, internal, moderate volume, must respect per-department access, must not guess.
- Data: HR policy docs, changing, access-controlled, freshness matters.
- Model: a mid-tier model is enough for grounded Q&A; large context not required if retrieval is good.
- Architecture: RAG with permission-filtered retrieval, grounded generation with citations, an output gate that refuses when unsupported.
- Eval: recall@k on policy-question pairs, faithfulness and citation correctness, sampled human review.
- Cost and latency: cache the system prompt, keep context tight, stream the answer.
- Risks: stale policy (track content age), unauthorized access (filter retrieval by department), hallucination (require citations, refuse if unsupported).

That is a complete answer in seven moves, each tied to the clarifying facts.

> **Interview.** Announce the framework, spend real time on clarify and data, keep the architecture the simplest thing that meets the bar, put evals before the build, and close with concrete risks and their guardrails. The structure itself is most of the score.

```recall
Q: What is the most common failure in an AI design interview?
A: Jumping to an architecture before clarifying scope and understanding the data. An elegant system that answers the wrong problem fails the question.
Q: Why do data questions come so early in the framework?
A: Most AI systems live or die on data. Whether knowledge is private, large, changing, and who may see it decides retrieval versus fine-tuning versus long context and surfaces permissions and freshness up front.
Q: What does placing a model on the latency, price, quality triangle mean in practice?
A: You cannot maximize all three. You pick a capability tier for the task and accept a trade: a faster cheaper model may cost quality, a higher-quality one costs latency or price. Select by eval, not leaderboard.
Q: Why should evals be discussed before the build, not after?
A: Evals define what good means and gate releases against regression. Without them you cannot tell whether an architecture or a later change actually works, so they come first in the design, not as an afterthought.
Q: How do you keep an architecture answer from over-engineering?
A: Prefer the simplest shape that meets the bar: a workflow before an agent, prompting before fine-tuning, retrieval before long context. Add complexity only when a named requirement forces it.
```
lessons.deeper:
## Looping, not marching

The seven steps are an order to open with, not a strict sequence. Real design is iterative: you reach the cost step and find the frontier model you chose blows the per-request budget, so you loop back to the model step and add a router, which changes the architecture to put a classifier in front. Or the risk step surfaces prompt injection on retrieved content, which pushes you back to architecture to isolate untrusted text and add an output gate. Signal this to the interviewer explicitly, say I am going back to the model choice because the cost budget just ruled out the frontier model everywhere, because it shows you understand the trade-offs connect rather than sit in separate boxes. A candidate who marches through the steps once and never revisits looks like they memorized a list; one who loops looks like they design.

## Making trade-offs out loud

The highest-signal thing you can do is reason about alternatives before committing. For each major choice, name the option you picked, the one you rejected, and why. RAG over long context here because the knowledge is large and changing and permissions matter. A workflow over an agent because the task is a fixed sequence and the loop would only add cost and failure modes. Prompting over fine-tuning because we have no evals yet and the base model may be enough. This is exactly what the stack-judgment and agents-versus-workflows lessons teach, applied live. The interviewer is listening for whether you can defend a decision against its alternative, not whether you landed on their preferred answer.

## Scoping to the time you have

A design question is time-boxed, so manage depth. Open with the full framework at a sentence each so the interviewer sees the whole shape, then go deep where they steer or where the problem is hardest, usually retrieval quality, the eval strategy, or the risk and guardrail layer. Explicitly defer the parts that are standard, I will assume a standard observability and tracing setup unless you want to dig in, so you spend the time on what differentiates a strong answer. Close by restating the design in three or four sentences and naming the one risk you are most worried about, which leaves the interviewer with a crisp summary rather than a half-finished diagram.
